notes.meaning: Peter quotes Psalm 16, which was written by King David. David described someone who lived with constant awareness of God, trusting the Lord at his right hand to protect him from being shaken. Peter explains that these words ultimately pointed to Jesus and His absolute trust in the Father.

differ.view: David was describing his own trust in God, and his experience was a picture of the Messiah's.
The psalm speaks of the Messiah alone. Making it mainly about David weakens Peter's whole argument.

notes.meaning: Because Jesus trusted His Father completely, His heart was full of gladness and His tongue praised God. He could face death knowing His physical body would rest in secure hope. He possessed the firm confidence that God would raise Him from the grave.

Hades here refers to the realm of the dead or the grave. Jesus truly died, but the Father did not leave Him trapped among the dead or permit His body to rot. Because Jesus was God's sinless Holy One, death could not keep hold of Him.

differ.view: Many understand Hades simply as the grave and the soul as the physical person, teaching that the verse guarantees Christ's body would not decay in the tomb.
Christ's human soul truly entered the realm of the departed spirits between His death and resurrection to continue His saving work, as stated in the Apostles' Creed.

notes.meaning: God guided Jesus through death and brought Him back into life through the resurrection. After rising, Jesus entered into heaven to experience the complete joy of the Father's presence. God will likewise guide all His followers along the path of eternal life.

Peter speaks with warmth and respect to his fellow Jews about their great ancestor David. Everyone in Jerusalem knew that David died, was buried, and his body remained in his tomb to that day. Because David's body decayed, he could not have been talking about himself escaping the grave.

David was an inspired prophet who looked ahead to God's solemn promise. God had sworn an unbreakable oath that one of David's descendants would sit on his royal throne forever. David understood that this promised King would rise from his own family line.

Guided by the Holy Spirit, David was looking forward to the resurrection of the Messiah. He prophesied that the Christ would not be abandoned in the realm of the dead and that His body would not rot. Jesus fulfilled this prophecy when He rose alive on the third day.

God brought Jesus of Nazareth back to life, fulfilling the promises made to David. Peter and the entire gathering of disciples were eyewitnesses who had seen, heard, and eaten with the risen Jesus. They boldly affirmed the historical truth of His resurrection.

After rising from the dead, Jesus ascended to heaven and was seated in supreme authority at God's right hand. Having received the Holy Spirit from the Father as promised, Jesus poured out the Spirit on the disciples. The unusual sounds and languages the crowd witnessed were visible proof of Jesus' heavenly rule.

David did not ascend bodily to heaven to sit beside the Father, so he was not talking about himself in Psalm 110. Instead, David called his promised descendant his Lord, recording God's command for Him to reign at His right hand. This reigning King will rule until every enemy is brought into total defeat.

Peter calls on the entire nation of Israel to know the truth with absolute certainty. The Father has given supreme power to Jesus, confirming Him as both the promised Messiah and the Lord of all creation. The very person they rejected and nailed to the cross has been exalted as ruler of the world.

When the crowd realized they had helped put God's Messiah to death, Peter's words pierced their consciences with sharp grief and guilt. They recognized their terrible danger and pleaded with the apostles to tell them what to do. Conviction of sin is the first step toward turning to God.

Repenting means changing one's mind and turning away from sin to follow Jesus. Peter told the people to show this inward change by being baptized in Jesus' name. God promised that if they turned to Christ, He would wash away their sins and give them the Holy Spirit.

differ.view: Baptism is an outward sign and seal of the covenant that points to Christ's cleansing, but it does not automatically give forgiveness apart from faith.
Repentance and personal faith alone bring pardon, and baptism is an outward expression of faith that follows forgiveness rather than causing it.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Water baptism is a sacrament necessary for salvation that washes away guilt and confers the gift of the Holy Spirit.

notes.meaning: God's offer of forgiveness and the Holy Spirit was not meant only for the people standing there that day. It extended to their descendants and to people far away, including the Gentiles. Every single person whom the Lord calls may receive these gifts.

differ.view: Because the covenant promise includes believers and their children, infants of Christian parents ought to receive baptism as the sign of entering God's covenant family.
The promise applies to children and those far off only as they grow up, hear the gospel, and personally respond to God's inward call with saving faith.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The promise extended to children demonstrates that the sacrament of baptism is not restricted to adults, supporting the baptism of infants.

notes.meaning: Peter did not stop with a brief sermon, but kept urging and teaching the crowd with many more words. He warned them to separate themselves from the unbelieving, rebellious culture around them to escape God's coming judgment. Turning to Christ requires leaving behind the ways of the world.

Those who gladly accepted Peter's preaching trusted in Jesus and were baptized in water. About three thousand people were added to the church that single day. The Holy Spirit brought a massive harvest of souls into God's family through one sermon.

differ.view: It is hard to picture three thousand people being fully dipped under water in the city in one day, so some may have been baptized another way, perhaps by sprinkling.
Jerusalem's many pools and ritual baths gave plenty of water to baptize that many people by dipping them under.

notes.meaning: The new believers spent their time learning God's truth from the apostles and building loving friendships with one another. They regularly broke bread together in shared meals and the Lord's Supper, and they met constantly for prayer. These spiritual habits kept the early church strong and faithful.

differ.view: 'Breaking of bread' may mean their ordinary shared meals, or meals followed by the Lord's Supper; we cannot be sure.

notes.meaning: A deep, holy awe fell upon the believers and the entire city because of God's powerful presence. The apostles performed many miraculous signs and wonders to confirm the truth of the gospel. God used this reverence to protect and establish the infant church.

The believers stayed closely united in heart, purpose, and regular meetings. Moved by spontaneous love for one another, they treated their belongings as common resources to be used for the good of all. True Christian love opens our hearts to share with others.

differ.view: This sharing was the natural fruit of love, and there is no proof Christ meant it to stop. If the church had kept that love, the practice would have continued.
This was an unusual case for that time and place, never commanded and not done elsewhere, so it is not a rule for all Christians. It still teaches that those with plenty should help the poor.

notes.meaning: Whenever church members noticed a brother or sister in need, they willingly sold pieces of land, houses, and goods to help. They divided the money among the poor so that everyone had enough food and shelter. Their generosity was voluntary and driven by compassion.

differ.view: This sharing was the natural fruit of love, and there is no proof Christ meant it to stop. If the church had kept that love, the practice would have continued.
This was an unusual case for that time and place, never commanded and not done elsewhere, so it is not a rule for all Christians. It still teaches that those with plenty should help the poor.

notes.meaning: The disciples gathered together every day in the temple courts for public prayer and worship. They also met in each other's homes to break bread and share meals with pure, joyful hearts. They carried a joyful spirit of worship into their everyday routines and family tables.

differ.view: Breaking bread at home included the Lord's Supper, which they shared daily.
Breaking bread here means ordinary shared meals at home, eaten with joy, not the Lord's Supper.

notes.meaning: The early Christians continually praised God, and their kind, upright lives earned the goodwill of the general public. Day after day, the Lord brought new converts into their fellowship as more people were saved from sin. A healthy, loving church naturally attracts others to the gospel.

differ.view: Those added were the people God had chosen for salvation, and God surely brings every one of them to Christ.
'Being saved' means people who were then being saved from the guilt and power of their sins. It does not mean everyone added was sure to be saved forever no matter what.
